etymology: Hebrew Chatsar ‘Enan, “the village of fountains” or “court of springs”; the north-eastern corner-mark of the promised land’s border in Num 34 and Eze 47.
biblical_def: Hazar-enan, the village of fountains, stands at the north-eastern corner of the land the LORD covenanted to Israel: “And the border shall go on to Ziphron, and the goings out of it shall be at Hazarenan: this shall be your north border” (Num 34:9). When Moses rehearsed the bounds of the inheritance, the line did not trail off into vagueness; it came to rest upon a named place, a corner-stake driven into the earth. Ezekiel, generations after, set the same fountain-village upon the restored map: “the border from the sea shall be Hazarenan…And this is the north side” (Eze 47:17). One obscure spring of water marks where the promise turns. Herein is a mercy for the pilgrim: the LORD measures the fulness of His people’s portion to the last landmark, and not one border of His word falls to the ground. He does not promise in the gross and default in the particulars. The heavenly Canaan, whereof the earthly was a shadow, is bounded by the same exactness — a city whose gates and foundations are numbered and sure. What the springs of Hazar-enan whispered to Israel the throne declares to the church: thine inheritance is appointed, staked, and kept. The saints shall possess it wholly, watered at its farthest edge, for the God who drew the line will bring them in.
webster_summary: The village of fountains at the north-eastern corner of the promised land’s border (Num 34:9; Eze 47:17); a witness that the LORD marks the fulness of His people’s inheritance to the last landmark.

Let the saint rest: the God who drew the line will bring His people into the whole of it.

etymology: Hebrew Sibrayim, of uncertain sense, perhaps “twofold hope” or “two hills”; a border-point between Damascus and Hamath in Ezekiel’s restored-land vision.
biblical_def: Between the border of Damascus and the border of Hamath, upon the renewed northern line of Ezekiel’s vision, lies Sibraim: “Hamath, Berothah, Sibraim, which is between the border of Damascus and the border of Hamath” (Eze 47:16). It is a small name set between two great ones, a marker the prophet did not omit though he might easily have passed it by. Therein the exactness of the LORD’s restoration is preached. When He brings again the captivity of His people and re-portions the land, He does it not by rough estimate but by the measuring line, naming each place, dividing to every tribe its due. The renewed inheritance is measured out down to Sibraim. This is the manner of our God in all His covenant dealings: He counteth the number of the stars, He putteth our tears into His bottle, He knoweth them that are His by name. Nothing of the promised portion is lost in the reckoning. The church, scattered and afflicted, may take heart that her restoration in Christ is no vague and general amnesty but a particular, measured, appointed inheritance — each ransomed soul set in its place, each border drawn by a faithful hand. What Sibraim, unnoticed of men, teaches is that the LORD forgets no landmark of His grace, and will bring His people into the whole of what He hath promised.

etymology: Hebrew Chatsar hattikon, “the middle village”; a settlement by the coast of Hauran on the restored northern line of Eze 47.
biblical_def: Hazar-hatticon, the middle village, stood by the coast of Hauran upon the restored border Ezekiel beheld: “Hazarhatticon, which is by the coast of Hauran” (Eze 47:16). A village set in the midst, a fold upon the frontier — and the prophet who saw the dry bones live saw also the fences of the inheritance raised again. Here the sure hope of the restored kingdom breaks forth. Israel had been driven out, her borders trampled, her cities emptied; yet the LORD, the good Shepherd of the scattered flock, purposed to gather them and re-fence the land they had lost. “I will feed them in a good pasture,” He said by this same prophet, “and upon the high mountains of Israel shall their fold be.” The middle village is one stake of that re-fenced fold. What the LORD did in figure for the northern tribes He does in truth for His whole church in Christ, who came to seek and to save that which was lost, and to gather together in one the children of God that were scattered abroad. Not one of His sheep is left beyond the border. He re-gathers the wandering, He restores the waste places, He sets every ransomed one within the fold. The restored kingdom is not a wish but a decree; and Hazar-hatticon, a village none remember, stands witness that the Shepherd fetches home His own.

etymology: Hebrew Berothah, “wells” or “cypresses”; a northern border-city, answering to the Berothai from which David took much brass (2Sa 8:8).
biblical_def: Berothah is named among the cities of the north border in Ezekiel’s survey of the land: “Hamath, Berothah, Sibraim…” (Eze 47:16), and answers to the Berothai from which David took exceeding much brass for the service of God. In the one place it is a landmark of the kingdom’s far reach; in the other, a spoil of the LORD’s wars adorning His house. Both preach the same thing. The dominion the LORD gave His anointed reached to the distant north, to cities the fathers had never trod, that Jeroboam in his day recovered again for Israel (2Ki 14:28); and the wealth of the vanquished was not squandered but sanctified, carried up to Jerusalem, poured into the vessels of the temple that God might be worshipped. So the far reach of the kingdom and the plunder of its wars alike serve the sanctuary. Herein is a shadow of the greater King, whose dominion shall be from sea to sea, who led captivity captive and received gifts for men, and who spoils the strong man’s house to enrich His own. Every stronghold Christ subdues He turns to the adorning of His church. Berothah, a border-city of brass, tells the saints that no corner of the earth lies beyond their King’s reach, and no spoil of His conquest is lost — all is gathered to the house and glory of God.

etymology: Hebrew Chethlon, perhaps “a hiding-place” or “wrapping”; the entering-point of the northern border, “the way of Hethlon” toward Zedad (Eze 47:15).
biblical_def: “The way of Hethlon” is the appointed entering-point of the northern border, where the line comes up from the great sea toward Zedad: “from the great sea, the way of Hethlon, as men go to Zedad” (Eze 47:15). It is not merely a place but a way — a road by which men enter the land. The Spirit names the passage, not the wilderness beside it. Herein lies a figure for the soul. The inheritance has an entering in; the true land is possessed by a way, and that way is not of man’s choosing but of the LORD’s appointing. There is a road into Canaan, and there is a road into heaven, and neither is many but one. “I am the way,” saith the Lord Jesus, “no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.” As Israel could not enter the promised bound save by the way of Hethlon marked out for them, so no sinner enters the rest of God save by the way that God hath set, even Christ crucified and risen. Men seek a thousand paths into blessedness, over the wall and through the hedge; but the strait gate and the narrow way alone lead unto life. The way of Hethlon rebukes every self-made entrance and points to the one door. Enter by it, and the whole inheritance is thine; refuse it, and thou art shut out, though the land lie in view.

etymology: Hebrew Tsedad, perhaps “a sloping place” or “the side”; a landmark of the north border named alike by Moses (Num 34:8) and Ezekiel (Eze 47:15).
biblical_def: Zedad is a landmark twice named, once by Moses and once by Ezekiel, standing upon the same north border across the long stretch of years between: “the goings forth of the border shall be to Zedad” (Num 34:8), and again, “the way of Hethlon, as men go to Zedad” (Eze 47:15). What Moses staked in the wilderness the prophet found still standing in the vision of the restored land. Herein the constancy of the LORD’s word is set forth. Kingdoms rose and fell, Israel sinned and was scattered, the border was overrun and the people carried far away; yet when God unrolled again the map of His mercy, the old landmark had not moved. Zedad in Ezekiel is Zedad in Numbers. The promise the LORD made through His servant did not weather away with the centuries, for heaven and earth shall pass away, but His words shall not pass away. Men’s covenants are written in sand and washed out by the next tide; the covenant of God is graven, and its landmarks stand. What He appointed to the fathers He keeps for the children. Let the saint who fears that the promise has grown old take Zedad for his comfort: the boundary-stone of grace is where the LORD first set it, and where He sets it, it abides. Not one word of all His good promise hath failed.

etymology: Hebrew Chamath, “fortress” or “defence”; the great Syrian city on the Orontes, and “the entering in of Hamath” the ideal northern limit of the land.
biblical_def: Hamath was the great city upon the river Orontes, and “the entering in of Hamath” the proverbial northern limit of the land — the point “as men come to Hamath” whither the spies searched (Num 13:21), which Jeroboam recovered for Israel (2Ki 14:28), and which Amos called “Hamath the great” (Amo 6:2). It marked the utmost bound the LORD had appointed for His people’s inheritance, the far gate of the promised portion. Yet the prophet named the city not to flatter but to abase the proud of Zion: pass ye to Hamath the great, and to Gath — be they better than these kingdoms? The men of Israel trusted in their own greatness, and Amos set the fallen glory of Hamath before them as a warning. For the great city that seemed a fixed and mighty bound was itself a thing the God of Israel weighed and found wanting; when Sennacherib boasted, “Where are the gods of Hamath?” (2Ki 18:34), her idols had already failed her. So the appointed border-city of pride was humbled before the living God, who setteth the bounds of the peoples and bringeth the great to nothing. Hamath teaches that no greatness of man — no city, no kingdom, no name — stands against the LORD, and that His people’s security is not in the strength of their borders but in the faithfulness of Him who drew them.

etymology: Hebrew Chamath Tsobah, joining Hamath with Zobah; the northern territory Solomon “went to…and prevailed against” (2Ch 8:3).
biblical_def: “And Solomon went to Hamathzobah, and prevailed against it” (2Ch 8:3). In a single sentence the chronicler records the reach of the peaceful king to the far northern territory, and his mastery over it. Solomon, whose name is peace, in the height of his glory subdued the distant borders, built store-cities in the land of Hamath, and extended the dominion of the anointed of the LORD unto regions the tribes had never held. Herein is a shadow, dim but true, of a greater Son of David. Solomon prevailed against Hamath-zobah by the sword; the true Prince of Peace prevails against the far kingdoms of the earth by His word and Spirit, going forth conquering and to conquer, until the uttermost parts are given Him for His possession. “He shall have dominion also from sea to sea, and from the river unto the ends of the earth.” What Solomon reached in figure Christ reaches in truth; no border is too far for His arm, no stronghold of Hamath too high for His throne. Before Him all nations shall be gathered (Mat 25:32), and every knee shall bow. The saint reading this brief and ancient conquest may lift up his heart: the King who prevailed at Hamath-zobah of old is prevailing still, and shall prevail, till the kingdoms of this world are become the kingdoms of our Lord and of his Christ.

The name marks where the region of Hamath met the land of Zobah.
Named once only, in 2Ch 8:3.
usage: Solomon went to Hamath-zobah and prevailed against it.
He built store-cities in the land of Hamath after his conquest.
Hamath-zobah shadows the dominion of the greater Son of David.

etymology: Hebrew Sepharvayim, “the two scribes” or “two books”; an Assyrian city whose deported people brought their gods and their child-sacrifice into Samaria.
biblical_def: Sepharvaim was a city of the Assyrian empire whence the king of Assyria brought men to people the emptied cities of Samaria: “from Sepharvaim, and placed them in the cities of Samaria instead of the children of Israel” (2Ki 17:24). These settlers did not come empty; they brought their gods, and with their gods their abominations, for “the Sepharvites burnt their children in fire to Adrammelech and Anammelech, the gods of Sepharvaim” (2Ki 17:31). Here the horror of idolatry stands naked. The idol is not a harmless custom nor a private preference; it is a devouring thing that demands the blood of children and consumes what it is given. The false gods of Sepharvaim could not save their own worshippers, and when Rabshakeh mocked, “Where are the gods of Sepharvaim…have they delivered Samaria out of mine hand?” (2Ki 18:34), the silence answered him. The dead idol delivers none, yet demands all. Against these bloody nothings stands the living God, who gave His own Son that He might not take ours, who abhors the burning of children and calls it that which He commanded not, neither came it into His heart. The living God against the dead idols of the nations — this is the great contest of the Scripture. Sepharvaim, with its fires and its cruel gods, warns every generation that whatever a man will not worship the LORD, he will worship a devourer.
webster_summary: The Assyrian city whose deported people brought their gods to Samaria and burnt their children in fire to Adrammelech and Anammelech (2Ki 17:24, 31); a witness against idolatry and the dead idols of the nations.
webster_full: SEPHARVAIM, an Assyrian city whose people were planted in Samaria.
Brought by the king of Assyria to fill the emptied cities (2Ki 17:24).
Its settlers burnt their children in fire to Adrammelech and Anammelech (2Ki 17:31).
Its gods could not deliver, as Rabshakeh mocked (2Ki 18:34).
A standing witness to the devouring cruelty of idolatry.
scriptures: And the king of Assyria brought men from Babylon, and from Cuthah, and from Ava, and from Hamath, and from Sepharvaim, and placed them in the cities of Samaria instead of the children of Israel: and they possessed Samaria, and dwelt in the cities thereof.
And the Avites made Nibhaz and Tartak, and the Sepharvites burnt their children in fire to Adrammelech and Anammelech, the gods of Sepharvaim.
Where are the gods of Hamath, and of Arpad? where are the gods of Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivah? have they delivered Samaria out of mine hand?
In the ninth year of Hoshea the king of Assyria took Samaria, and carried Israel away into Assyria, and placed them in Halah and in Habor by the river of Gozan, and in the cities of the Medes.
corruption_summary: The Assyrian city of Adrammelech and Anammelech, whose people burnt their children in fire; a naked witness to the abomination of idolatry.
corruption_paragraphs: Sepharvaim names a genuine corruption, and the Scripture does not soften it. Its people were planted in Samaria and there burnt their children in fire to Adrammelech and Anammelech, the gods of Sepharvaim (2Ki 17:31). The idol is no innocent custom; it is a devourer that demands the blood of the innocent and gives no deliverance in return. When Rabshakeh boasted that the gods of Sepharvaim had not saved their own city, the silence of those dead idols was their whole answer.

Against these bloody nothings stands the living God, who abhors the burning of children and calls it a thing He commanded not, neither came it into His heart. He gave His own Son that He might not require ours. The great contest of the Scripture is the living God against the dead idols of the nations, and it is not ended: whatever a man will not worship the LORD, he will worship a devourer. The principle to recover is undivided worship of the one true God, and the utter renouncing of every idol that consumes its worshippers.
roots_summary: The name has been read as a dual, “the two scribes” or “two books,” from a root akin to sepher, a book or writing.
roots_lines: Sepharvaim — Hebrew Sepharvayim, a dual form.
Linked to sepher, a book, scroll, or writing.
Hence read as “the two scribes” or “twin cities of books.”
Its people are called the Sepharvites (2Ki 17:31).
Its gods were Adrammelech and Anammelech, honoured with fire.
usage: The king of Assyria brought men from Sepharvaim into Samaria.
The Sepharvites burnt their children in fire to their gods.
Rabshakeh asked where the gods of Sepharvaim were.

etymology: Greek Dalmanoutha, of uncertain and disputed sense; an obscure region by the sea of Galilee, near Magdala, named once only (Mar 8:10).
biblical_def: After He had fed the four thousand and sent the multitude away, “straightway he entered into a ship with his disciples, and came into the parts of Dalmanutha” (Mar 8:10) — an obscure coast by the sea of Galilee, so little known that no other page of Scripture names it, and no eye of man has since surely found it. Yet the incarnate Lord came thither. This is the wonder of the gospel of Galilee: the King of glory walks the little places, the unregarded shores, the villages of no report. He does not confine His presence to Jerusalem and the great; He comes to Dalmanutha. And straightway, the Evangelist tells, the Pharisees came forth seeking of Him a sign from heaven, tempting Him — the ancient sin of unbelief, that will not have the Christ who is present unless He perform on demand. He sighed deeply in his spirit, and gave them no sign but departed. So grace passes through the obscure coast, offered and refused: welcomed by the multitude fed, spurned by the learned who sought a wonder. Let the reader mark where the Lord is found — not where men look for spectacle, but in the plain word and the humble place. Dalmanutha, a nameless shore, held the Saviour of the world; and the sign-seeker, wanting proof, missed the Presence that was standing before him.
webster_summary: The obscure region by the sea of Galilee to which Christ came after feeding the four thousand, where the Pharisees sought a sign (Mar 8:10); a witness that grace passes through the little places, and unbelief misses the Presence.
webster_full: DALMANUTHA, an obscure region by the sea of Galilee.
Thither Christ came by ship after feeding the four thousand (Mar 8:10).
Named once only in all the Scripture, near Magdala.
There the Pharisees sought of Him a sign, tempting Him.
A witness that grace visits the humble place, and unbelief misses the Lord.

corruption_summary: The nameless Galilean coast where Christ came and the Pharisees sought a sign; it recovers the humility of grace and the rebuke of sign-seeking unbelief.
corruption_paragraphs: An unknown shore by the sea of Galilee, named but once, kindles no controversy of the present age. Its wonder is that the incarnate Lord came thither at all, honouring the little places with His presence while the great cities went their way.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is where the Lord is truly found. The Pharisees at Dalmanutha demanded a sign from heaven and were given none; unbelief, wanting spectacle, missed the Presence standing before it. Grace is met not in the demand for wonders but in the plain word and the humble place. Mark where Christ walks, and follow Him there.
roots_summary: The Greek name is of disputed derivation, perhaps rendering an Aramaic place-name; some connect it with a sense of a harbour or heights near Magdala.
roots_lines: Dalmanutha — Greek Dalmanoutha, of uncertain origin.
Thought to render an underlying Aramaic name.
The parallel place in Matthew is called Magdala.
Set among “the parts of Dalmanutha” by the sea of Galilee (Mar 8:10).
Named once only in all the Scripture.
usage: Christ came into the parts of Dalmanutha by ship.

Dalmanutha, a nameless coast, held the Saviour of the world.
